title: Government & Democracy · Episode 1
chapters: The social contract: why we agree to be governed
Left, right and the big political ideas

units.t: Government & Democracy. Episode one.
In this episode: How democracy works, The social contract: why we agree to be governed and Left, right and the big political ideas.
Part one. How democracy works.
Rule by the people sounds simple.
For most of history it was rare, fragile and limited.
Here's how it grew, and what actually keeps it alive.
Rule by the people.
Democracy comes from the Greek demos, the people, and kratos, power.
Authority comes from citizens, not a monarch, priesthood or military.
In a direct democracy citizens vote on decisions themselves.
In a representative democracy they elect people to decide for them, and can remove them at the next election.
Almost every democracy today is mainly representative, with some direct elements.
Athens is the best-known early example, but not the only one.
Ancient Indian texts describe republics such as the Vajji confederacy, where councils of clan leaders debated and voted around the 500s BC, though only an elite took part.
In Iceland, Norse settlers founded the Althing in 930, often called one of the world's oldest surviving parliaments.
In two small Swiss cantons, citizens still vote on laws by raising their hands.
From Rome to the ballot.
After Athens, rule by the people largely faded for centuries, but pieces survived.
The Roman Republic elected magistrates and had a Senate, though wealthy families dominated.
In England, Magna Carta in 1215 established that even the king was bound by law, and parliaments gradually won control over taxation.
A civil war and the Glorious Revolution of 1688 left Parliament stronger than the monarch.
This Westminster model later shaped Australia, Canada and New Zealand.
Enlightenment thinkers such as John Locke argued that governments get legitimacy from the consent of the governed.
The American Revolution of 1776 and French Revolution of 1789 placed this at the centre.
Early electorates were small, often limited to propertied men.
Over the next century and a half the vote widened to working men, women and groups excluded by race.
Universal suffrage is surprisingly recent.
Australian experiments.
The Australian colonies were busy laboratories of democracy.
In 1870 Victoria began paying members of parliament, so working men, not just the wealthy, could afford to serve.
In 1899 Queensland's Anderson Dawson became premier of what is usually described as the world's first Labour government, though it lasted only about a week.
Tasmania trialled the Hare-Clark system of proportional representation in Hobart and Launceston in the 1890s and adopted it statewide in 1909.
It is still used there and in the ACT.
And in 1921 Edith Cowan won a seat in Western Australia, becoming the first woman elected to an Australian parliament.
Voting directly.
Pure direct democracy is impractical for a nation of millions, but elements survive.
Switzerland is the best-known example: citizens vote on national questions several times a year, and can force a vote on a new law by gathering enough signatures.
Many US states let citizens put proposals on the ballot.
In Australia, the main direct element is the constitutional referendum: the Constitution can only be changed if voters approve.
Supporters say direct votes give people real ownership of big decisions.
Critics warn that complex issues can be reduced to slogans and that turnout and information vary.
What keeps it working.
Holding elections doesn't guarantee a working democracy.
Elections must be free and fair, run by an independent body, with secret ballots and real choice.
The rule of law means everyone, including leaders, answers to the same laws through independent courts.
A free press and free speech let citizens learn what government does and criticise it without fear.
Minority protections stop the majority overriding others' basic rights.
And losers must accept the result.
Churchill told Parliament in 1947 that it had been said democracy is the worst form of government except for all the others tried.
It can be slow and frustrating, but it lets mistakes be corrected and leaders replaced without violence.
Citizens keep it alive by voting thoughtfully, checking political claims, contacting their local member and respecting those who vote differently.
The key idea: Democracy means citizens hold ultimate power, either deciding directly or electing representatives, and its roots reach well beyond Athens.
Part two. The social contract: why we agree to be governed.
Why should anyone obey the government?
For nearly four centuries, philosophers have answered with a powerful thought experiment: imagine life with no rulers at all, then ask what deal reasonable people would strike.
Hobbes: war of all.
Picture waking to find no police, courts, laws or government.
Nothing would stop a stronger neighbour taking your food or home.

This imagined situation is the 'state of nature', the starting point of the social contract: the idea that governments are legitimate because the governed, in some sense, agree to them, trading some freedom for security and order.
Thomas Hobbes lived through the English Civil War.
In Leviathan, 1651, he argued that people in a state of nature would be roughly equal in their ability to harm one another, and constantly suspicious.
The result: a war of every person against every person, with no farming, industry or arts, and life 'solitary, poor, nasty, brutish, and short'.
The only escape was a single sovereign strong enough to keep the peace.
Even a harsh ruler beat chaos.
Locke and natural rights.
John Locke painted a gentler picture.
In Two Treatises of Government, around 1689, he argued that even in a state of nature people are bound by a natural law forbidding harm to others' life, health, liberty or possessions.
People form governments not to escape chaos but to protect these rights more reliably, with impartial judges and enforcement.
That changes everything.
A government built to protect rights can lose its legitimacy by violating them, and people may then resist and replace it.
His ideas about consent and natural rights echoed in the American Declaration of Independence in 1776, which speaks of unalienable rights to life, liberty and the pursuit of happiness.
Rousseau and the general will.
Geneva-born Jean-Jacques Rousseau took the idea in another direction.
His book The Social Contract, 1762, opens with the line usually translated as 'Man is born free, and everywhere he is in chains.'
He thought existing societies had corrupted people and entrenched inequality.
A legitimate society, he argued, is one where citizens collectively make their own laws, guided by the general will: what is genuinely in the common interest, not just the sum of private wants.
In obeying such laws, people would in effect obey themselves.
His ideas inspired democratic and revolutionary movements, especially in France.
Critics worried the general will could be twisted to justify forcing people to conform.
But did anyone sign.
The obvious objection is that no one ever signed anything.
You were born into a country with laws already in place.
In the 18th century the Scottish philosopher David Hume argued that most governments began in conquest or usurpation, not agreement.
Some theorists replied that by staying and accepting a country's benefits, you give tacit consent.
Hume answered that this is like saying a man carried aboard a ship while asleep consents to the captain because he could leap into the ocean.
Later critics, including some feminist scholars, argued that historical versions of the contract quietly excluded women and colonised peoples from the agreement altogether.
Rawls and the veil.
In 1971 the American philosopher John Rawls revived the idea in A Theory of Justice, not as history but as a test of fairness.
Imagine designing a society from behind a veil of ignorance, not knowing whether you would be rich or poor, talented or not, or which gender, race or religion you would have.
Rawls argued you would choose equal basic liberties and accept inequality only if it benefits the least advantaged.
In 1974 his Harvard colleague Robert Nozick countered that people's rights to what they have earned strictly limit what a state may redistribute, defending a much smaller government.
These debates echo in arguments over taxes, welfare and trading freedom for safety.
When someone claims authority over you, ask whether the people affected could genuinely agree to it.
The key idea: Hobbes argued that without a powerful ruler, life would be a constant war of fear and conflict.
Part three. Left, right and the big political ideas.
Why do we say 'left' and 'right'?
The answer involves a French assembly hall in 1789, and the ideas that grew from it still shape every election.
Where left and right began.
The words left and right began in France in 1789, in the early months of the Revolution.
In the National Assembly, members who wanted to keep strong powers for the king, such as a royal veto over laws, sat to the right of the presiding officer.
Those who wanted more radical change sat to the left.
The seating habit stuck.
Today the labels are shorthand for several questions bundled together.
On economics, the left generally favours more government action to reduce inequality, through taxes, welfare and public services.
The right generally favours lower taxes, freer markets and more reliance on individual effort.
On social questions, the left is often linked with faster change and the right with preserving tradition.
The bundles don't always hold together, and the labels shift between countries and eras.
Liberals and conservatives.
Liberalism grew from Enlightenment thinkers such as John Locke, who argued that people have natural rights to life, liberty and property, and that government rests on consent.
Classical liberals stressed free markets, free speech and limited government.
Social liberals later argued that real freedom also needs education, health care and a safety net.
Conservatism is often traced to Edmund Burke's 1790 warning against tearing down institutions for abstract theory.
Conservatives hold that customs, families and long-standing institutions carry accumulated wisdom, so change should be careful and gradual.
Critics say this can defend unfair arrangements simply because they are old.
Beware the word 'liberal': in the United States it signals the centre-left, but Australia's Liberal Party sits on the centre-right.
Socialists and libertarians.
Socialism emerged in the 1800s in response to the harsh conditions of the Industrial Revolution.
Socialists argue that wealth is produced collectively, so key industries should be owned or controlled by the public and shared more equally.
Communist states built one-party, centrally planned systems.
Democratic socialists instead seek change through elections, with strong unions, public services and welfare inside a market economy.
Critics point to communist failures and weakened incentives.
Libertarians want people free to live as they choose, so long as they don't harm others, under the smallest possible state.
That mixes free markets, which sounds right-wing, with personal freedoms, which can sound left-wing.
Critics say a minimal state would leave the vulnerable unprotected and struggle with shared problems like pollution.
Beyond a single line.
Because one line mixes up too many questions, some people use two axes.
The horizontal axis measures economic views, from more state control on the left to more free market on the right.
The vertical axis measures personal freedom, from authoritarian, favouring strong state control of behaviour, to libertarian, favouring minimal control.
American libertarian David Nolan drew an early version, and the online Political Compass quiz made the idea widely known.
Even two axes simplify reality.
Environmentalism, nationalism and populism cut across these lines in different ways, and political scientists still debate how best to map beliefs.
Thinking fairly.
Every major political tradition contains serious thinkers responding to real problems.
Liberty, fairness, stability and security all matter, and people weigh them differently.
A useful habit is to describe an opposing view so well that its supporters would agree with your summary, sometimes called steelmanning.
Be wary of labels used as insults, and check whether a claim about 'the other side' describes its mainstream or its fringe.
Most people's views are a mix, and they change over a lifetime.
Understanding the ideas, rather than just the teams, makes political debate more useful.
The key idea: Left and right come from the French Assembly of 1789 and now loosely describe views on equality, the economy and the pace of change.
Quick recall. Answer out loud, or just in your head.
Question one. What is the main difference between direct and representative democracy?
Answer. Citizens decide directly, or elect others to decide.
Question two. Why did Hobbes think people should accept a powerful ruler?
Answer. It prevents constant fear and conflict.
Question three. On economic questions, what does the left generally favour?
Answer. More government action to reduce inequality.
That's the end of this episode. The questions are waiting in your review, so you can lock in what you heard.
